### record `binding-record`

One device node's binding, as DeviceManager holds it.  The node is stable from the boot scan onward, so a record exists for a device nothing binds - which is a fact about the machine and not an absence.

| field | type | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bus` | `u32` |  |
| `dev` | `u32` |  |
| `func` | `u32` |  |
| `generation` | `u64` | The claim generation of the current binding, or of the last one that ended. 0 for a node that has never been claimed. |
| `state` | `binding-state` |  |
| `cause` | `failure-cause` |  |
| `attempts` | `u32` | Automatic attempts spent on the current incident. |
| `artifact` | `string` | The driver artifact chosen for it, or empty where nothing matched. |
| `rule` | `u32` | WHICH of that entry's match rules chose it. An entry may declare several - a kind and a pinned address, say - and "virtio_console bound it" does not say which of them applied. `system-manifest` refuses two entries whose rules overlap at one priority, so the artifact and this index together name the rule uniquely. |
| `providers` | `u32` | How many providers this binding has published. |
| `resources` | `u32` | How many resources the bind granted it - the MMIO window, an interrupt, and whatever its registry entry asked for. |

### record `provider-info`

One published provider, named by the identity DeviceManager assigned it - never by one a driver chose. The binding is its publisher's: the PCI function's bus/device/ function and the claim generation of the binding that published it, so a provider from a binding that is over is distinguishable from its replacement. `slot` and `provider-generation` are the manager's own, and together they make a reused slot unmistakable for the provider that left it.

| `func` | `u32` |  |
| `binding-generation` | `u64` |  |
| `slot` | `u32` |  |
| `provider-generation` | `u32` |  |

### enum `policy-verb`

What an operator may do to a binding. FOUR VERBS, and the fourth arrived because a state nothing can leave is not a policy - it is a way to lose a device until the next boot.  Only `disable` and `select` are PERSISTENT. A retry is an action, not a stored preference; and `enable` is not a third stored state but the REMOVAL of the disable record, so a device that was never disabled and one that was enabled again are the same device.

| case | ordinal | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `disable` | 0 | Turn it off. Persists. |
| `enable` | 1 | Turn it back on: deletes the disable record rather than storing a third state. |
| `select` | 2 | Prefer one of the candidates the registry ALREADY declared. Persists. Applies at the NEXT bind - rebinding a live device because a preference changed would take a working driver away at a moment nobody chose. |
| `retry` | 3 | Try this binding again, now. An action; nothing is stored. |

### enum `policy-outcome`

What a verb did, or why it did not.

| case | ordinal | description |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `accepted` | 0 | It was accepted and, where the verb persists, written. |
| `no-such-device` | 1 | The device index names no node. |
| `not-a-candidate` | 2 | `select` named an artifact the registry never declared for this device. Policy NARROWS and never widens, so a preference the registry did not offer is refused rather than obeyed. |
| `quarantined` | 3 | `retry` on a quarantined binding. Its resources are charged and out of circulation precisely because nothing confirmed the device was quiet, and an operator saying so does not make it so. `disable`, `enable` and `select` are still accepted on one, because they are about the NEXT bind. |
| `busy` | 4 | An `enable` arriving while a disable's teardown is still in flight. The operator retries once the node reaches `disabled`; cancelling the intent would mean a device that was never observed to be disabled at all, which is worse to explain than a refusal that says why. |
| `refused` | 5 | The verb reached a node it cannot apply to - a boot-critical binding, whose policy would live on a volume that is not mounted when that binding is made. |
| `not-stored` | 6 | It could not be written down. The binding is unchanged, which is what a failed write must mean rather than a change nothing recorded. |

## Interfaces

### interface `device`

The Device service contract: enumerate the devices the kernel discovered on the bus, or look one up by its table index. Typed enumeration over the kernel device table (the same table DeviceManager binds drivers to).

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `list` | `list() -> result<list<device-entry>, error>` |  |
| 2 | `get` | `get(index: u32) -> result<device-entry, error>` |  |
| 3 | `bindings` | `bindings() -> result<list<binding-record>, error>` | The binding of every device node, FORWARDED VERBATIM from DeviceManager - which is the only process that holds them. Not derived here: a second rendering is how one surface comes to report a constant where a state belongs, and `lsdev` and the System Graph must not be able to disagree about what a device is doing. |

### interface `device-policy-admin`

The operator's endpoint. NARROW ON PURPOSE: holding `CAP_CONFIG`, or holding the read-only binding snapshot, gets a component no closer to it - it is minted for the operator path and for nothing else, the way every other operator authority in this tree is reached.  The division is the whole of the authority question: DeviceManager owns the DECISION and exposes these four verbs; ConfigService holds the bytes under a prefix DeviceManager alone writes. A component that can write the config file therefore cannot change a binding.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `apply` | `apply(index: u32, verb: policy-verb, artifact: string) -> result<policy-outcome, error>` |  |
| 2 | `stored` | `stored(index: u32) -> result<string, error>` | What is stored for this device right now, so an operator can see a preference before a reboot applies it. |

### interface `provider-catalogue`

The provider catalogue, served by DeviceManager - the only process that holds it.  `subscribe` answers with everything of that kind published RIGHT NOW and continues as the live stream. One operation, because two would have a window between them: a provider added after the read and before the registration would be in neither, and that is the same race as a service started later seeing nothing.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `subscribe` | `subscribe(kind: provider-kind) -> stream<provider-info>` |  |
| 2 | `bindings` | `bindings() -> list<binding-record>` | Every device node's binding, in one read. `lsdev` and the System Graph both ask this rather than each deriving a state - the log is not a third rendering to compare against, because it is a history of transitions and this is a moment. |

### interface `usb`

The USB bus contract, served by the xHCI driver itself (the owner of the bus state): enumerate the devices it addressed, live - hot-plugged and detached devices come and go from the list. The `lsusb` inventory reads this.

Request `[op u16][corr u32][args]`, reply `[corr u32][result]`.

| op | method | signature | description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `list` | `list() -> result<list<usb-device>, error>` |  |
